title: H1B to Canada RSU Tax Guide: Navigate Stock Vesting After Returning Home

## The H1B to Canada RSU Problem

### You Thought You Were Done with US Taxes

You worked at Meta in California for 3 years on H1B. You got a 4-year RSU grant worth $400,000 ($100K/year). You returned to Vancouver in year 3.

**Your assumption:**
"I'm back in Canada. The US can't tax me anymore."

**Reality:**
Both countries want to tax your Year 4 RSU vesting:

- **US position:** "You earned 75% of those RSUs while working here (3 years / 4 total). We tax 75%."
- **Canada position:** "You're a Canadian resident when they vest. We tax 100%."

**Result:** You pay tax to **both countries** on the same $100,000.

Without proper planning, your effective tax rate on Year 4 vesting can hit **72%** (36% US + 36% Canada).

But there's a solution.

### How RSU Vesting is Sourced Between Countries

RSU income is allocated based on **where you worked during the vesting period**, not where you live when they vest.

**Formula:**
```
US-sourced % = (Days worked in US / Total days in vesting period)
Canada-sourced % = (Days worked in Canada / Total days in vesting period)
```

**Example: Meta 4-Year Grant**

Grant date: January 1, 2022  
Vest schedule: 25% per year (1095 days each)  
Work history:
- Jan 1, 2022 - Dec 31, 2023: Menlo Park (730 days)
- Jan 1, 2024 - Dec 31, 2024: Menlo Park (365 days)
- Jan 1, 2025 - Dec 31, 2025: Vancouver (365 days)

**Year 4 vesting (Jan 1, 2026):**
```
Total vesting period: 1,461 days (Jan 2022 - Jan 2026)
Days in US: 1,095 days (2022-2024)
Days in Canada: 366 days (2025)

US-sourced: 1,095 / 1,461 = 75%
Canada-sourced: 366 / 1,461 = 25%
```

On $100,000 vesting:
- US claims: $75,000
- Canada claims: $25,000

**Important:** This is sourcing, not taxation. Both countries may tax more due to worldwide income rules.

---

## US Taxation of RSUs After You Leave

### You're No Longer a US Resident

Once you return to Canada and cut substantial ties to the US, you become a **non-resident alien** for tax purposes.

**What this means:**
- File **Form 1040-NR** (not Form 1040)
- Only report **US-sourced income** (not worldwide)
- Use different tax brackets (no standard deduction)
- No QBI deduction, no Child Tax Credit, limited itemization

### Withholding on RSU Vesting

Your employer (Meta, Google, Amazon) will still withhold taxes when RSUs vest:

**Standard withholding:**
- Federal: **22%** (supplemental wage rate)
- State: **13.3%** (if California-sourced)
- FICA: **0%** (non-resident aliens exempt from Social Security/Medicare)

Total: **35.3%** withheld automatically

**Example: $100,000 vesting (75% US-sourced)**
```
Gross vesting: $100,000
US-sourced: $75,000

Withholding:
Federal (22%): $16,500 ($75K × 22%)
California (13.3%): $9,975 ($75K × 13.3%)
FICA: $0 (non-resident exempt)

Total withheld: $26,475
Net proceeds: $73,525
```

**Problem:** Is 35.3% withholding enough?

**Answer:** Usually no. Your actual tax liability is higher.

### Actual US Tax Liability

**Federal tax on $75,000 US-sourced:**

Using 2026 non-resident tax tables:
```
First $11,600: 10% = $1,160
Next $33,150: 12% = $3,978
Next $30,250: 22% = $6,655

Total federal: $11,793
```

But wait—there's a quirk. Non-residents pay tax on **gross income** with limited deductions.

If you have no US deductions (no mortgage, no state tax deduction), you pay on the full amount:

**Effective rate:** 15.7% ($11,793 / $75,000)

But if you're in a high income year (multiple vestings, bonuses), you hit higher brackets:

**Top bracket (37%):** Kicks in at $243,725

On $300,000 vesting (75% US = $225,000):
```
Federal tax: ~$70,000 (31% effective)
```

**State tax:**
California doesn't care if you're a non-resident. They tax based on sourcing:
```
CA-sourced: $75,000
CA rate: 13.3% (top bracket)
CA tax: $9,975
```

**Total US tax:**
- Federal: $11,793
- California: $9,975
- **Total: $21,768** (29% effective rate)

**Withholding gap:**
- Withheld: $26,475
- Actual tax: $21,768
- **Refund: $4,707**

In this case, you're **over-withheld**. You get a refund when you file Form 1040-NR.

But if your total income is higher, you might be **under-withheld** and owe money.

## Canadian Taxation of RSUs

### You're a Canadian Resident

As a Canadian resident, you pay tax on **worldwide income** including:
- RSUs vesting (even if from US employer)
- US brokerage interest
- US stock sales
- Canadian income (salary, rental, RRSP withdrawals)

### Canadian Tax on $100,000 RSU Vesting

**Scenario:**
You have $50,000 Canadian salary + $100,000 RSU vesting.

**Total income:** $150,000 CAD (converting USD to CAD at 1.36)

**Federal + BC tax:**
```
First $55,867: 20.05% = $11,201
Next $55,866: 29.65% = $16,564
Next $38,267: 37.16% = $14,220

Total tax: $41,985
Effective rate: 28%
```

But wait—can you claim Foreign Tax Credit for US taxes paid?

### Foreign Tax Credit Calculation

**Yes!** You can claim FTC to avoid double taxation.

**Form T2209 calculation:**
```
Foreign tax paid (US): $21,768 USD × 1.36 = $29,605 CAD
Canadian tax on foreign income: $41,985
FTC limit: Lesser of:
  1. Foreign tax paid: $29,605
  2. Canadian tax on foreign income: $41,985

FTC claimed: $29,605

Net Canada tax: $41,985 - $29,605 = $12,380
```

**Total tax paid:**
- US: $21,768 USD
- Canada: $12,380 CAD ($9,103 USD)
- **Combined: $30,871** (30.9% effective rate)

You paid tax **once** to the US, then paid the difference to Canada (since Canada's rate is higher).

**Key point:** You don't pay tax twice on the same dollar. FTC ensures you pay the **higher of the two rates**.

## California's Aggressive RSU Sourcing

### The CA 540-NR Trap

California doesn't let you off the hook just because you left.

**Rule:** California sources RSU income based on **where you worked during vesting**, even if you no longer live there.

**You must file CA Form 540-NR** (non-resident return) every year until all RSUs vest.

**Example:**
- Worked in CA: 2022-2024 (3 years)
- Moved to Vancouver: January 2025
- 4-year RSUs vest: 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025

**2025 vesting:**
```
RSU value: $100,000
CA sourcing: 3 years work / 4 year vest = 75%
CA taxable: $75,000
CA tax (13.3%): $9,975
```

You live in Canada but owe California **$9,975**.

**What if you don't file CA 540-NR?**

California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) will:
1. Receive Form W-2 from your employer (showing CA-sourced income)
2. Notice you didn't file
3. Send a bill 2-3 years later
4. Add **25% penalty** + **10% interest** + **$135 late-filing penalty**

**Your $9,975 bill becomes:** $14,300

And FTB is **aggressive**. They'll garnish wages, freeze bank accounts, file liens.

**Solution:** File CA 540-NR every year, even if you owe $0.

### Other High-Tax States to Watch

**New York (10.9% top rate):**
- Similar sourcing rules
- File NY IT-203 (non-resident return)
- "Convenience rule" can claim you're still a NY employee if you work remotely

**Massachusetts (9% flat rate):**
- Sources RSU based on work performed
- File MA Form 1-NR/PY

**Oregon (9.9% top rate):**
- Sources RSU based on work location
- File OR Form 40N

**No-income-tax states (better!):**
- Washington, Texas, Florida, Nevada, Alaska, Wyoming, South Dakota, Tennessee
- No non-resident filing (nothing to source)
- Only federal tax applies

## Strategies to Minimize RSU Tax

### Strategy 1: Accelerate Vesting Before You Leave

Some employers (Meta, Amazon) allow early vesting if you're leaving the company.

**Example:**

You're returning to Canada in December 2025. You have:
- $100,000 unvested RSUs (vesting in 2026, 2027, 2028)

**Option A (default):** Let them vest naturally
- 2026 vesting: 50% US-sourced, 50% Canada-sourced → Tax rate: 40-50%
- 2027 vesting: 25% US-sourced, 75% Canada-sourced → Tax rate: 45-52%
- 2028 vesting: 0% US-sourced, 100% Canada-sourced → Tax rate: 49.8%

**Option B (accelerate):** Request vesting before you leave
- All vesting in November 2025 (while US resident)
- 100% US-sourced → Tax rate: 36-40%
- **Savings:** 10-12 percentage points = $30,000-36,000

**How to request:**
1. Talk to your manager ("I'm relocating to Canada for family reasons")
2. Contact equity admin (Equity Edge, Shareworks, E*TRADE)
3. File written request citing relocation

**Success rate:** ~60% for Meta/Amazon, ~20% for Google (depends on manager discretion)

### Strategy 2: Delay Your Move to Q2

If you have a large Q1 vesting, delay your Canada move by 3 months:

**Scenario:**
- RSU vesting: $150,000 on February 15, 2026
- Planned move: January 2026
- **Revised move:** April 2026

**Tax impact:**

**Original plan (move in Jan):**
```
US-sourced: 75% = $112,500
Canada-sourced: 25% = $37,500

US tax: $112,500 × 36% = $40,500
Canada tax: $150,000 × 50% - FTC = $34,500
Total: $75,000 (50% effective)
```

**Revised plan (move in Apr, after vesting):**
```
US-sourced: 100% = $150,000
Canada-sourced: 0%

US tax: $150,000 × 36% = $54,000
Canada tax: $0 (wasn't Canadian resident yet)
Total: $54,000 (36% effective)
```

**Savings:** $21,000 (14 percentage points)

Is a 3-month delay worth $21,000? For most people, yes.

### Strategy 3: RRSP Mega-Contribution

When you return to Canada with RSU income, max out your RRSP:

**Scenario:**
- RSU vesting in 2026: $100,000
- RRSP room: $50,000 (accumulated from previous years)

**Without RRSP:**
```
Canadian taxable income: $100,000
Canadian tax: $49,800 (49.8%)
```

**With RRSP:**
```
Contribute: $50,000 to RRSP (by March 1, 2027)
Taxable income: $50,000
Canadian tax: $20,000 (40%)
Tax savings: $29,800

Effective RRSP return: $29,800 / $50,000 = 59.6%
```

You get a **59.6% immediate return** on your RRSP contribution.

**Catch:** You need **$50,000 cash** to contribute. Where do you get it?

**Answer:** Sell some of the vested RSUs to fund the RRSP contribution.

**Net result:** Convert RSU income (taxed at 50%) into RRSP savings (59.6% return) = **9.6% arbitrage**.

### Strategy 4: Sell RSUs Before Leaving US

RSU vesting triggers **ordinary income tax**. Selling after vesting triggers **capital gains tax**.

**Key difference:**
- US capital gains (long-term): **20%** max
- Canadian capital gains: **50% inclusion** × 49.8% rate = **24.9%** effective

**Strategy:** Sell all vested RSUs **before** you leave the US:

**Example:**

You have $200,000 of vested RSUs (already taxed at ordinary income rates). Current value: $250,000.

**Gain:** $50,000

**Option A (sell before leaving US):**
- US capital gains tax (short-term): 37% × $50,000 = $18,500

**Option B (sell after moving to Canada):**
- Canadian capital gains: 50% × 49.8% × $50,000 = $12,450

**Difference:** $6,050 saved by selling in Canada.

But wait—there's more:

If you **hold for 1 year** before selling (long-term capital gains):

**Option A (sell in US after 1 year):**
- US long-term gains: 20% × $50,000 = $10,000

**Option B (sell in Canada after 1 year):**
- Canadian capital gains: 24.9% × $50,000 = $12,450

**Difference:** $2,450 saved by selling in US.

So the strategy depends on your holding period:
- **Short-term:** Sell in Canada (24.9% vs 37%)
- **Long-term:** Sell in US (20% vs 24.9%)

## Filing Requirements: The Checklist

### US Tax Returns

**Form 1040-NR (Non-Resident Alien Income Tax Return)**

Due: **June 15** (you get automatic 2-month extension since you live abroad)

**Required attachments:**
- Schedule NEC (Tax on Income Not Effectively Connected with US Business)
- Form 8833 (Treaty-Based Return Position—if claiming treaty benefits)
- Form 8840 (Closer Connection Exception—if you spent 183+ days but claim Canadian residence)

**State returns:**
- CA 540-NR (non-resident)
- NY IT-203 (non-resident)
- [Your state]-NR

Due: Same as federal (usually April 15, but June 15 for non-residents)

### Canadian Tax Returns

**Form T1 (General Income Tax Return)**

Due: **April 30** (or June 15 if self-employed)

**Required schedules:**
- Schedule 3: Capital gains/losses
- Form T2209: Federal foreign tax credits
- Form T1135: Foreign income verification (if foreign property > $100K CAD)

**Provincial return:** Automatically generated from T1

### Foreign Account Reporting

**FBAR (FinCEN Form 114)**

Required if aggregate foreign accounts > **$10,000** at any point during the year.

**What counts for Canadians:**
- US bank accounts (checking, savings)
- US brokerage accounts (E*TRADE, Fidelity, Schwab)
- US 401(k) / IRA

Due: **April 15** (automatic extension to October 15)

Filed: **Separate from tax return** (FinCEN website)

**Form T1135 (Canadian Foreign Income Verification)**

Required if foreign property > **$100,000 CAD**.

**What counts for US residents:**
- Unvested RSUs (if value > $100K)
- US stock holdings
- US 401(k) balance

Due: **April 30** (with Form T1)

## Real Case Study: Google L5 → Vancouver

**Profile:**
- Joined Google 2022: $200K salary + $600K RSU (4-year vest: 5/15/20/60)
- Location: Mountain View, California
- Returned to Vancouver: July 1, 2025
- Final year vesting: $360,000 (60% of grant) on August 15, 2026

### Tax Calculation: Year 4 Vesting

**Vesting details:**
- Grant date: January 1, 2022
- Vest date: August 15, 2026 (1,687 days after grant)
- Work split:
  - US: Jan 1, 2022 - July 1, 2025 = 1,277 days
  - Canada: July 1, 2025 - Aug 15, 2026 = 410 days

**Sourcing:**
```
US-sourced: 1,277 / 1,687 = 75.7% = $272,520
Canada-sourced: 410 / 1,687 = 24.3% = $87,480
```

**US Tax (Form 1040-NR):**
```
US-sourced income: $272,520
Federal tax (35% effective): $95,382
CA state tax (13.3%): $36,245
Total US tax: $131,627
```

**Canadian Tax (Form T1):**
```
Total RSU income (CAD): $360,000 × 1.36 = $489,600
Other income: $30,000 (part-year salary)
Total income: $519,600

BC tax (before FTC): $519,600 × 49.8% = $258,760

Foreign Tax Credit:
US tax paid: $131,627 × 1.36 = $179,013 CAD
FTC limit: $258,760
FTC claimed: $179,013

Net Canada tax: $258,760 - $179,013 = $79,747 CAD
```

**Total Tax Paid:**
- US: $131,627
- Canada: $79,747 CAD ($58,638 USD)
- **Combined: $190,265** (52.9% effective rate)

**Net proceeds:** $360,000 - $190,265 = **$169,735**

### What If They Used Strategy 1?

Request early vesting in June 2025 (before leaving US):

**Tax impact:**
```
Vest date: June 15, 2025 (still US resident)
US-sourced: 100% = $360,000
Canada-sourced: 0%

US tax:
Federal (37%): $133,200
CA state (13.3%): $47,880
Total: $181,080

Canada tax: $0 (wasn't Canadian resident)

Total tax: $181,080 (50.3% effective)
```

**Savings:** $190,265 - $181,080 = **$9,185**

By requesting early vesting, they saved $9,185 (2.6 percentage points).

Not huge, but worth a 30-minute conversation with their manager.

## Common Mistakes H1B Returnees Make

### ❌ Mistake 1: Not Filing CA 540-NR

You worked in CA, moved to Canada, stopped filing CA tax returns.

**3 years later:** CA FTB sends a bill for $40,000 + $10,000 penalties.

**Why:** California had the right to tax your RSU income (work-period sourcing).

**Cost:** $10,000 in avoidable penalties.

### ❌ Mistake 2: Not Claiming Foreign Tax Credit

You paid $30,000 to the US, then paid $50,000 to Canada (no FTC claimed).

**Result:** Paid $80,000 total (double taxation).

**Should have paid:** $50,000 (US tax + difference in Canada).

**Cost:** $30,000 overpaid.

### ❌ Mistake 3: Filing Form 1040 Instead of 1040-NR

You're a Canadian resident but filed Form 1040 (US resident return).

**Result:** IRS taxes your worldwide income (Canadian salary, RRSP, TFSA, rental).

**Cost:** $15,000-40,000 in extra tax.

### ❌ Mistake 4: Not Tracking Work Days

You can't remember exactly when you moved. You guess "50/50" for sourcing.

**Reality:** You worked 85% of vesting period in the US.

**Result:** Under-report US income, IRS assesses penalties.

**Cost:** $5,000 in penalties + interest.

### ❌ Mistake 5: Selling RSUs at Wrong Time

You vest RSUs in the US (ordinary income tax paid), move to Canada, then sell 2 years later.

**Result:** Canadian capital gains tax (24.9%).

**Should have:** Sold in US after 1 year (20% long-term capital gains).

**Cost:** 4.9 percentage points × $100,000 gain = $4,900.

## Your Action Plan

### 3 Months Before Returning to Canada

- [ ] Review all unvested RSUs (pull equity statements)
- [ ] Calculate US vs Canada sourcing for each future vest
- [ ] Request early vesting (if employer allows)
- [ ] Decide: vest before leaving or after?
- [ ] Run scenarios with our [calculator](/us-canada-tax-calculator)

### 1 Month Before Move

- [ ] Sell vested RSUs (if beneficial for capital gains treatment)
- [ ] Max out 401(k) contributions (you can't contribute after leaving)
- [ ] Notify employer of Canadian residence (for withholding updates)
- [ ] Update W-4 to reflect final year status
- [ ] Close TFSA (if you had one before moving to US)

### After Moving to Canada

- [ ] Track exact move date (critical for sourcing calculations)
- [ ] Open RRSP account (prepare for contributions)
- [ ] Set up Canadian bank account
- [ ] Notify CRA of residency change (Form RC325)

### At Tax Time (Year 1 in Canada)

**US returns:**
- [ ] File Form 1040-NR (non-resident return)
- [ ] File CA 540-NR (or other state non-resident return)
- [ ] Report only US-sourced income
- [ ] File by June 15

**Canadian returns:**
- [ ] File Form T1 (first-year Canadian resident)
- [ ] Report worldwide income (including US RSUs)
- [ ] Claim Foreign Tax Credit (Form T2209)
- [ ] File Form T1135 (if foreign property > $100K)
- [ ] File by April 30

### Every Year Until RSUs Fully Vest

- [ ] Continue filing US 1040-NR (if you have US-sourced RSU income)
- [ ] Continue filing CA 540-NR (for California sourcing)
- [ ] Continue claiming FTC in Canada
- [ ] Keep records: vesting dates, amounts, FX rates, work days

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Do I still owe US tax after moving to Canada?

Yes, on **US-sourced income** (RSUs earned while working in US). You file Form 1040-NR every year until all equity vests.

### Can I avoid California tax by moving?

No. California sources RSU based on **where you worked**, not where you live. You file CA 540-NR until all equity vests.

### How long do I file US tax returns?

Until you have **no US-sourced income**. For most H1B returnees: 1-4 years (until all RSUs vest).

### Can I contribute to RRSP with RSU income?

Yes! RSU income counts as "employment income" for RRSP purposes. Use it to maximize your contribution.

### Should I keep my 401(k) or transfer to RRSP?

**Keep it.** 401(k) has treaty protection (Article XVIII). Transferring to RRSP triggers US tax and loses treaty benefits.

### What if my employer won't accelerate vesting?

Use **Strategy 2**: Delay your move to Canada until after large vestings. This keeps income 100% US-sourced (lower tax).

Returning to Canada with unvested RSUs is **complex but manageable**:

✅ **Understand sourcing rules** (work-period allocation)  
✅ **File both US and Canadian returns** (until all equity vests)  
✅ **Claim Foreign Tax Credit** (avoid double tax)  
✅ **Time your move strategically** (around large vestings)  
✅ **Max out RRSP** (convert high-tax RSU income to tax-deferred savings)  

The average H1B returnee with $400K unvested RSUs pays **$210,000 in taxes** over 4 years.

With proper planning, you can reduce this to **$175,000**.
